course: Cosmetics: Lip Balms, Body Butters & Hair Oils

lessons.title: Calculating Cost of Goods Sold for Each Product
lessons.body: To know if you are making a profit, you must first know exactly what each product costs you to make. This is called Cost of Goods Sold (COGS). COGS includes every ingredient and packaging item that goes directly into one unit of your product. For example, if you make a 50g tin of body butter, you need to add up the cost of shea butter, coconut oil, essential oil, the tin, and the label. Suppose you buy 1kg of shea butter for 5000 Naira. You use 30g per tin. That's 150 Naira. Coconut oil: 1 litre for 2000 Naira, you use 20ml, so 40 Naira. Essential oil: 10ml for 1500 Naira, you use 5 drops (about 0.25ml), so 37.50 Naira. The tin costs 100 Naira, label 20 Naira. Total COGS per tin = 150 + 40 + 37.50 + 100 + 20 = 347.50 Naira. Round to 348 Naira. You must do this for every product: lip balm, hair oil, etc. Keep a notebook or use a simple Excel sheet on your phone. List all ingredients and packaging, their purchase price, and the amount used per unit. Then divide the purchase price by the number of units you can make from that purchase. For instance, if a 500g bag of beeswax costs 3000 Naira and you use 5g per lip balm, then cost per balm = (3000/500)*5 = 30 Naira. Be precise. Don't forget small items like pipettes, gloves, or cleaning supplies that are used per batchâthese are overheads, not COGS, but they affect your total cost. COGS is only the direct materials. Once you have COGS per unit, you can set a price that covers all costs and gives profit. Without accurate COGS, you might think you're making money when you're actually losing. Review your COGS every time supplier prices change. In Africa, prices fluctuate, so update monthly. Use a simple formula: COGS = sum of (cost of ingredient / amount used per unit). This is the foundation of all pricing decisions.

lessons.title: Setting Wholesale and Retail Prices
lessons.body: Once you know your Cost of Goods Sold (COGS), you can set your wholesale and retail prices. Wholesale is the price you sell to shops or resellers who buy in bulk. Retail is the price you sell directly to consumers, usually at markets or online. A common rule is to multiply COGS by 2 for wholesale and by 3 or 4 for retail. For example, if your body butter COGS is 348 Naira, wholesale price = 348 x 2 = 696 Naira. Retail price = 348 x 3 = 1044 Naira, round to 1000 Naira for simplicity. This gives you a profit margin. But you must also consider what the market will pay. In many African markets, customers are price-sensitive. Check what similar products sell for in your local market or on Jumia. If your retail price is too high, you may not sell. If too low, you won't cover overheads and profit. For wholesale, you need to offer a discount to resellers so they can make a profit too. They will typically double the wholesale price to set their retail. So if you sell wholesale at 700 Naira, they sell at 1400 Naira. That might be too high. So adjust: maybe wholesale 600 Naira, retail 900 Naira. Your profit per unit at wholesale = 600 - 348 = 252 Naira. At retail = 900 - 348 = 552 Naira. You need to decide how much you want to earn. Also consider production volume: selling 100 units at 200 Naira profit each gives 20,000 Naira, while selling 50 units at 500 Naira profit gives 25,000 Naira. Sometimes lower price with higher volume is better. But never sell below COGS. That's a loss. Set a minimum price. Also, offer tiered wholesale pricing: buy 10-49 units at 700 Naira, 50-99 at 650, 100+ at 600. This encourages larger orders. Always communicate your prices clearly. Use a price list. Review prices every 3-6 months as costs change. Remember, your time is also valuableâinclude a labor cost in your pricing if you pay yourself. But for now, focus on materials and overhead. With practice, you'll find the sweet spot where customers buy and you profit.

lessons.title: Managing Overhead Costs
lessons.body: Overhead costs are all the expenses that are not directly tied to making a specific product. They include rent for your workspace, electricity, internet, transportation to buy supplies, packaging materials for shipping, marketing, and even your own salary if you pay yourself. These costs must be covered by your sales, or you will not be profitable. To manage overhead, first list every overhead expense you have each month. For example: rent for a small room = 20,000 Naira, electricity = 5,000 Naira, data/internet = 3,000 Naira, transport = 4,000 Naira, marketing (flyers, social media ads) = 5,000 Naira. Total overhead = 37,000 Naira per month. Now you need to allocate this overhead to each product. If you produce and sell 200 units per month, overhead per unit = 37,000 / 200 = 185 Naira. Add this to your COGS to get total cost per unit. So body butter total cost = 348 + 185 = 533 Naira. Then your retail price of 1000 Naira gives profit of 467 Naira. But if you only sell 100 units, overhead per unit = 370 Naira, total cost = 718 Naira, profit only 282 Naira. So increasing sales volume reduces overhead per unit. To manage overhead, look for ways to reduce costs: share a workspace with another entrepreneur, buy packaging in bulk, use free social media instead of paid ads, combine trips to the market. Keep track of all overhead expenses in a notebook or app like Excel or a simple expense tracker. At the end of each month, compare total overhead to total sales. If overhead is more than 30% of sales, you need to cut costs or increase prices. Also, avoid unnecessary expenses. Every Naira saved on overhead is extra profit. Remember, overhead is fixed in the short term, so you must sell enough to cover it. Set a target: sell at least enough units to cover overhead + COGS + desired profit. This is your break-even point. Calculate it: break-even units = total overhead / (price - COGS). For body butter: 37,000 / (1000 - 348) = 37,000 / 652 = 57 units. So you must sell at least 57 units to cover overhead. Beyond that, profit starts. Manage overhead tightly, and you'll be more profitable.

lessons.title: Creating Bundles and Special Offers
lessons.body: Bundles and special offers are powerful ways to increase sales and profitability. A bundle is when you combine two or more products and sell them at a slightly lower price than if bought separately. For example, a 'Lip Care Bundle' with one lip balm and one body butter. If lip balm COGS is 150 Naira and body butter COGS is 348 Naira, total COGS = 498 Naira. If you sell them separately, retail might be 500 Naira for lip balm and 1000 Naira for body butter, total 1500 Naira. A bundle price of 1300 Naira gives the customer a 200 Naira discount, but you still make profit: 1300 - 498 = 802 Naira profit, compared to 1500 - 498 = 1002 Naira if sold separately. You sacrifice 200 Naira but may sell more bundles because of the perceived value. Bundles also move slow-selling products. For instance, if hair oil is not selling well, bundle it with a popular body butter. Special offers include 'Buy 2 Get 1 Free' or 'Free delivery for orders above 5000 Naira'. These can boost sales volume. But be careful: 'Buy 2 Get 1 Free' means you give away one unit. If your profit margin is 50%, giving one free may wipe out profit on the other two. Calculate: if each unit profit is 500 Naira, selling 2 gives 1000 Naira profit, but giving one free costs you 348 Naira (COGS), so net profit = 652 Naira. Still positive, but lower. Only run such offers if you can afford it and if it brings in new customers. Another popular offer is 'First 10 customers get 10% off'. This creates urgency. Use social media to announce offers. In Africa, WhatsApp status and Facebook groups are great for this. Also, create holiday bundles for Christmas, Ramadan, or Valentine's Day. Track which offers work by recording sales before, during, and after. Don't run too many offers at once, or customers will wait for discounts. Use bundles to increase average order value. If a customer buys one lip balm for 500 Naira, offer a bundle of 3 for 1200 Naira instead of 1500. They save 300 Naira, you sell more. Always ensure your bundle price covers COGS + overhead + profit. Never bundle at a loss. With creativity, bundles can significantly boost your income.

lessons.title: Tracking Expenses and Income
lessons.body: To run a profitable cosmetics business, you must track every Naira that comes in and goes out. This is called bookkeeping. Without it, you won't know if you're making a profit or loss. Start simple: get a notebook and divide each page into two columns: 'Income' and 'Expenses'. Or use a free app like Excel, Google Sheets, or a mobile app like 'Expense Manager'. Record every sale immediately: date, product, quantity, amount. For example, '5 Jan 2025, 3 body butters, 3000 Naira'. Record every expense: ingredients, packaging, transport, rent, data, etc. For example, '5 Jan 2025, shea butter 1kg, 5000 Naira'. At the end of each week, total income and expenses. Subtract expenses from income to get profit. If profit is negative, you spent more than you earned. You need to adjust. At the end of the month, do a full review. Calculate your total revenue, total COGS, total overhead, and net profit. Your net profit = revenue - (COGS + overhead). For example, if you sold 100 body butters at 1000 Naira each, revenue = 100,000 Naira. COGS per unit = 348 Naira, total COGS = 34,800 Naira. Overhead for the month = 37,000 Naira. Net profit = 100,000 - 34,800 - 37,000 = 28,200 Naira. That's your profit. Now you can see if you're meeting goals. Also track inventory: how many units you have left. This helps you plan production. Keep receipts for all purchases. Even if you buy from a local market without a receipt, write it down. Use a separate bank account or mobile money wallet for business to avoid mixing personal and business funds. At the end of each month, reconcile: does your cash balance match your records? If not, find the discrepancy. Tracking helps you identify problems early: maybe a particular product is not selling, or an ingredient cost has risen. You can then adjust prices or find cheaper suppliers. It also helps when applying for loans or grants. Remember, what gets measured gets managed. Make tracking a daily habit. Spend 10 minutes each evening to record the day's transactions. Over time, you'll have a clear picture of your business's financial health.

lessons.title: Scaling Production for Higher Profit
lessons.body: Scaling production means making more products to sell more and increase profit. But scaling requires planning. First, ensure your current production is profitable and you have steady demand. If you sell 100 units a month and consistently sell out, you can scale. To scale, you need to increase efficiency. Buy ingredients in bulk to reduce cost per unit. For example, if you buy shea butter in 25kg drums instead of 1kg bags, the price per kg drops. Suppose 1kg costs 5000 Naira, but 25kg drum costs 100,000 Naira, which is 4000 Naira per kg. That saves 1000 Naira per kg. For 100 body butters using 30g each, you need 3kg, saving 3000 Naira. That's extra profit. Also, negotiate with suppliers for discounts. Buy packaging in larger quantities. Invest in simple equipment: a digital scale, a hand mixer, a sealing machine. These reduce labor time and increase output. For example, a sealing machine can seal 100 lip balm tubes in 10 minutes instead of 1 hour by hand. That frees you to make more products or sell. Consider hiring one or two assistants to help with production and packaging. Pay them fairly, but ensure the increased output covers their wages. For example, if you pay an assistant 20,000 Naira per month, they must help you produce at least 40 extra units (at 500 Naira profit each) to cover their cost. That's 10 units per week. Usually, an assistant can help you double production. Also, standardize your recipes so anyone can follow them. Write down exact measurements and steps. This ensures consistency. When scaling, you may need a larger workspace. Look for a small production room or share with others. Marketing must also scale: use social media ads, attend trade fairs, approach more shops for wholesale. Keep tracking expenses and income as you grow. Reinvest a portion of profits into more inventory and equipment. Don't scale too fastâincrease gradually. If you double production, make sure you can sell the extra units. Otherwise, you'll have dead stock. Set a goal: increase production by 20% each month. With careful planning, scaling can significantly increase your profit and turn your small business into a thriving enterprise.

quiz.q: What does COGS stand for?
quiz.explanation: COGS is the direct cost of producing the goods you sell.

quiz.q: Which of the following is included in COGS for a body butter?
options: B) Shea butter used in the product
quiz.explanation: COGS includes only direct materials like ingredients and packaging, not overheads.

quiz.q: If 1kg of shea butter costs 5000 Naira and you use 30g per tin, what is the shea butter cost per tin?
quiz.explanation: 5000 Naira / 1000g = 5 Naira per gram; 5 x 30g = 150 Naira.

quiz.q: Why is it important to calculate COGS accurately?
options: B) To know the minimum price you can sell at without losing money
quiz.explanation: Accurate COGS helps you set prices that cover costs and yield profit.

quiz.q: How often should you update your COGS?
quiz.explanation: Prices fluctuate, so update COGS regularly to reflect current costs.

quiz.q: What is a common rule for setting wholesale price?
quiz.explanation: A common practice is to double COGS for wholesale to cover overhead and profit.

quiz.q: If your body butter COGS is 348 Naira, what is a typical retail price using a 3x markup?
quiz.explanation: 3 x 348 = 1044 Naira, often rounded to 1000 Naira.

quiz.q: Why might you set a lower price than the 3x markup?
options: B) To match market prices and increase sales volume
C) Because customers don't like high prices
quiz.explanation: Market conditions and competition may require a lower price to attract buyers.

quiz.q: What is a tiered wholesale price?
options: A) Same price for all quantities
B) Lower price for larger quantities
C) Higher price for larger quantities
D) Price based on customer's location
quiz.explanation: Tiered pricing encourages bigger orders by offering discounts for volume.

quiz.q: What should you never do when setting prices?
quiz.explanation: Selling below COGS guarantees a loss on each unit.

quiz.q: Which of these is an overhead cost?
quiz.explanation: Overheads are indirect costs like rent, not direct materials.

quiz.q: If total overhead is 37,000 Naira and you produce 200 units, what is overhead per unit?
quiz.explanation: 37,000 / 200 = 185 Naira per unit.

quiz.q: How can you reduce overhead per unit?
quiz.explanation: Spreading fixed overhead over more units lowers the per-unit overhead.

quiz.q: What is break-even point?
options: A) When you make maximum profit
B) When total revenue equals total costs
C) When you sell at a loss
D) When you have no sales
quiz.explanation: Break-even is the point where you cover all costs but make no profit yet.

quiz.q: If overhead is 37,000 Naira, price is 1000 Naira, and COGS is 348 Naira, how many units to break even?
What is a bundle?
options: A) A single product sold at full price
B) Two or more products sold together at a discount
quiz.explanation: Bundles combine products to increase value and sales.

quiz.q: Why create bundles?
options: B) To increase average order value and move slow-selling items
D) To avoid selling individual items
quiz.explanation: Bundles encourage larger purchases and help clear inventory.

quiz.q: If lip balm COGS is 150 Naira and body butter COGS is 348 Naira, what is total COGS for a bundle of both?
What is a risk of 'Buy 2 Get 1 Free'?
options: B) It may reduce profit if margins are low
C) It attracts too many customers
quiz.explanation: Giving a free unit costs you COGS, which can eat into profit.

quiz.q: How can you test if a special offer is working?
options: A) Track sales before, during, and after the offer
quiz.explanation: Tracking sales data shows the offer's impact on revenue and profit.

quiz.q: Why is tracking expenses and income important?
options: A) To know if you are making a profit or loss
quiz.explanation: Tracking gives you a clear picture of your business's financial health.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool for tracking?
quiz.explanation: A notebook or a simple spreadsheet app works well for beginners.

quiz.q: If you sold 100 body butters at 1000 Naira each, what is your revenue?
Net profit is calculated as:
quiz.explanation: Net profit subtracts all costs (COGS and overhead) from revenue.

quiz.q: Why keep business and personal money separate?
options: A) To avoid confusion and track business performance accurately
quiz.explanation: Separating funds makes it easier to see true business profit.

quiz.q: What does scaling production mean?
options: B) Making more products to increase profit
quiz.explanation: Scaling means increasing output to meet demand and grow profit.

quiz.q: How can buying in bulk help when scaling?
options: A) It increases cost per unit
B) It reduces cost per unit
quiz.explanation: Bulk buying often lowers the price per unit of ingredients.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of investing in simple equipment like a sealing machine?
options: B) It reduces labor time and increases output
C) It makes products more expensive
quiz.explanation: Equipment speeds up production, allowing you to make more units.

quiz.q: If you hire an assistant for 20,000 Naira per month, how many extra units at 500 Naira profit each must they help produce to cover their cost?
quiz.explanation: 20,000 / 500 = 40 units to break even on the assistant's wage.

quiz.q: What is a good practice when scaling?
options: A) Scale as fast as possible
B) Increase production gradually and ensure demand
quiz.explanation: Gradual scaling with demand ensures you don't overproduce.
